paper_title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Our starting point was ordinary. We picked POPE [Li et al., 2023] to benchmark hallucinationmitigation idea of our own, and the first step was to reproduce the LLaVA-1.5-7B [Liu et al., 2023] baseline. Running the model in 4-bit on single NVIDIA RTX 3070 Ti gave us 82.21 F1 on POPE adversarial. The adversarial baselines we meant to beat sat at 73.54, 79.30, and 81.00. We looked at the evaluation code and found readout choice that moves F1 on its own: two-token logit-readout pattern. Whether any published method used it we could not confirm (Section 4). The pattern grabs the first generated token, then labels it by comparing two logits, ℓ3582 for yes against ℓ1217 for no. We logged the argmax token on all 9,000 of our runs. Token 3582 appeared 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: VLM4RWD. ...ASSISTANT: LLaMA tokenizer (SentencePiece) generates Yes (ID 3869) or No (ID 1939) 2-token check IDs {3582, 1217} no match wrong decision yes-rate = 0.760 F1 = 0.761 (adv.) adversarial = 6.13 F1 points 8-token check IDs {3582, 8241, 4874, 3869, 1217, 3782, 694, 1939} matches correctly correct decision yes-rate = 0.452 F1 = 0.822 (adv.) Figure 1: Decision path at the POPE answer position for LLaVA-1.5-7B. The model always emits space-prefixed surface form ( Yes or No). The two-token check inspects two IDs the model never produces in this context, so every comparison is between two candidates the decoder excluded. On the adversarial split that comparison reads 924 of the models 1,644 No answers (56%) as yes, pushing the yes-rate to 0.760 on 50% positive split. zero times. Token 1217 also appeared zero times. What the model does produce, every single time, is token 3869 ( Yes, space-prefixed) for yes answer and token 1939 ( No, space-prefixed) for no. The reason is mechanical. The LLaMA-2 SentencePiece tokenizer [Kudo and Richardson, 2018, Touvron et al., 2023] glues whitespace byte onto word-initial tokens in mid-sentence position, and the ASSISTANT: suffix leaves the answer word exactly there. IDs 3582 and 1217 are perfectly valid vocabulary entries. They simply never surface after ASSISTANT: under greedy decoding in this model. Under greedy decoding the model never emits ID 3582 or 1217 at the answer position, so the twotoken rule compares two candidates the decoder excludes. Take the 1,644 adversarial questions the model answers No on: the 3582 logit beats the 1217 logit on 924 of them. Of those, 660 sit on true-negative questions and flip into false positives; the remaining 264 sit on borderline label-yes questions and become true positives. Borderline positives flip at 0.810 and true negatives at 0.501, so the excluded logits may still track the models lean, and we call the failure candidate exclusion. The yes-rate climbs to 0.760, recall inflates to 0.9587, and F1 sinks to 0.7608. Figure 1 follows the path end to end. Nothing in the models behaviour changed. The same generated tokens, read under the eight-token rule, produce different aggregate. The 6.13-point shift matters because it exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed, and none of those papers states which readout produced its baseline. That leaves the published comparison open. Setting our 82.21 beside another papers baseline would not give corrected gain, because our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization and published baseline may differ from it in readout, precision, prompt format, or decoding. We report what each paper states and leave the comparison unresolved until those factors are matched. We then turned the eight-token protocol on our own ideas and ran nine inference-time corrections, six grounding-based and three contrastive. Every one finished below 0.8221. The reasons are specific, and Appendix walks through them with per-question diagnostics. These corrections and the attention probe (Appendix F.3) are secondary findings, and the readout audit does not depend on them. Three claims organize the paper. Section 3 documents the space-prefixing behaviour across all 9,000 questions and traces how the protocol error propagates into reported metrics. Section 4 tabulates the baselines and gains that published methods report and explains why they cannot be set against ours until readout and precision are matched. Section 5 extends the audit to four additional VLMs and shows the confound is property of the readout, not of any one model. Extended derivations, the nine failed corrections, the formal equivalence proof, and the full literature survey live in the appendix.

sections.title: 2 Background
sections.content: 2.1 The POPE benchmark Li et al. [2023] proposed POPE as polling alternative to open-ended caption hallucination metrics, where drawing clean binary correctness line is awkward. Each poll shows one image and one target object and asks: Is there {object} in the image? Three negative-sampling strategies give three splits. Random draws absent objects uniformly from COCO [Lin et al., 2014]. Popular picks the most frequent COCO objects that happen to be missing from the queried image. Adversarial picks objects that co-occur with objects that are present (a snowboard scene gets asked about skis; kitchen scene gets asked about refrigerator). Every split holds 3,000 questions, balanced 50/50 between yes and no. The distinction that matters for our claim is how the yes/no answer gets read off, and POPE-style evaluation admits several readouts. We separate four. (i) The official POPE benchmark [Li et al., 2023], which we treat as the dataset plus the metric definition (yes/no F1, precision, recall, and yes-rate over the balanced splits). (ii) String-parsing evaluation, where generation step produces text and the label is recovered by searching for yes or no; this is blind to which LLaMA token ID the model chose. (iii) two-token logit readout, comparing the first-token logits at IDs 3582 and 1217. We do not claim the official POPE code mandates this readout, and we could not verify the readout of any published baseline we survey (Section 4). (iv) Our eight-token logit readout, which adds the alternate-case and space-prefixed forms so the comparison reads tokens the tokenizer actually emits after ASSISTANT:. 2.2 LLaVA-1.5 and its tokenizer LLaVA-1.5 [Liu et al., 2023] wires CLIP-ViT-L/14-336 vision encoder [Radford et al., 2021] to Vicuna-1.5-7B through two-layer MLP. Vicuna-1.5 descends from LLaMA-2 [Touvron et al., 2023], whose SentencePiece subword tokenizer [Kudo and Richardson, 2018] handles word boundaries by prepending whitespace byte to word-initial tokens in mid-sentence position. So Yes owns two IDs in the LLaMA vocabulary: 8241 for the start-of-sentence variant (Yes) and 3869 for the mid-sentence variant ( Yes). The same split holds for yes (3582 vs. 4874), No (3782 vs. 1939), and no (1217 vs. 694). The LLaVA-1.5 template ends with the literal string ASSISTANT:, so the next token is mid-sentence, the space byte is prepended, and the model emits 3869 or 1939. Appendix lists the raw decode outputs. 2.3 Evaluation-protocol sensitivity Scores that drift with measurement choices are familiar problem in NLP evaluation. Liang et al. [2022] showed benchmark numbers move visibly with prompt format and few-shot setup; Zheng et al. [2023] traced answer-ordering bias in LLM-as-judge protocols. Our finding belongs to that family: small, unexamined detail of how evaluation reads model output quietly becomes load-bearing for downstream comparisons. We keep the scope explicit. The conditions are LLaMA-family tokenizer, the ASSISTANT: template, and greedy decoding. Methods that run generation and parse the output string are not touched by the two-token readout. Methods that inherit the two-ID lookup are, by an amount that tracks the share of the negative split the model answers no on (Eq. 1).

sections.title: 4 Comparability with Published Results
sections.content: Table 3 lists the baseline, result, and gain that each surveyed paper reports for LLaVA-1.5-7B on POPE. None of these papers states which readout it used, and we do not hold their per-question logs, so the table cannot tell us whether given baseline came from the two-token logits, the eight-token set, or parsed generated text. Our 82.21 cannot stand in for those baselines either. It ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, and the published numbers may come from higher-precision runs, so gap between our reference and published baseline would mix the readout effect with precision difference. The table therefore computes no gain against 82.21 and assigns no readout to any paper. The adversarial gains in the table range from +0.70 to +10.81. Five of the six papers report less than the 6.13 points by which the readout alone moved our adversarial F1; Tang et al. report +10.81. The adversarial baselines run from 73.54 (Tang et al.) to 82.07 (Jana et al.), spread of 8.53 points on one frozen checkpoint, and the baselines of Tang, Seo, and Chen (73.54, 79.30, 81.00) already span 5 Table 4: POPE F1 under the four readouts for four VLMs beyond the LLaVA-1.5-7B reference (top block, from Table 2). legacy_2tok and legacy_8tok hard-code the LLaVA-1.5 LLaMA-2 IDs; dynamic_single re-derives the single-token yes/no IDs from each models own tokenizer; string_parse greedily decodes and parses the first yes/no substring. sections.title: 5 Multi-Model Validation
sections.content: The audit so far concerns one model. To separate LLaVA-1.5 quirk from readout property, we ran the identical four-readout audit on four more VLMs spanning three tokenizer families: LLaVA-1.6Mistral-7B (Mistral vocabulary), InstructBLIP-Vicuna-7B and mPLUG-Owl2-LLaMA2-7B (LLaMA family), and Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct (Qwen vocabulary). Each model saw all three splits at 3,000 questions per split, 9,000 per model. LLaVA-1.6-Mistral ran locally (RTX 3070 Ti Laptop, 4-bit NF4, transformers v4.44.2); the other three ran on Kaggle Tesla T4 GPUs under the same audit script. Qwen2-VL used its native chat template, since it was never trained on the LLaVA-1.5 prompt string; the other three used the LLaVA-1.5 template. Table 4 is the headline result, and two patterns hold across every model and split. 1. Porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim is unsafe, and how badly it fails depends on the target vocabulary. The legacy_8tok readout scores F1 0.00 on LLaVA-1.6-Mistral and Qwen2-VL: their vocabularies put no yes/no mass on those IDs, so comparison between two never-generated logits resolves the same way every time. On mPLUG-Owl2 and InstructBLIP, both LLaMA-family models that share the IDs, the fixed set still works. The failure is vocabulary mismatch, not something universal. 2. readout derived from each models own tokenizer is robust. The dynamic_single readout, comparing max-logits over the single-token yes/no IDs the tokenizer actually produces, stays 6 between 0.80 and 0.92 on every model and split. The spread across models is genuine accuracy variation, not an artifact of the readout. The string_parse column matches dynamic_single to four decimals on LLaVA-1.6-Mistral, mPLUGOwl2, and Qwen2-VL. On InstructBLIP it collapses to the 0.6667 all-yes floor across all three splits while dynamic_single holds at 0.82 to 0.88. The cause is the parse, not the model: the text our harness decoded for InstructBLIP did not begin with the answer token, so the first yes/no substring came from the wrong place. Appendix contains the token-ID map, the prompt-template robustness check, provenance notes, and the secondary verification run.

sections.title: 6 Practitioner Recommendations
sections.content: The audit reduces to handful of checks that any POPE-style evaluation on LLaMA-family VLMs can adopt without touching the dataset, the model, or the metric. 1. Log the generated token ID and its decoded string for every question. first-token argmax and its surface form are cheap to record and remove any need to guess the readout convention afterwards. 2. Verify the yes/no token sets under the exact prompt template. Different suffixes push firsttoken mass onto different forms. The ASSISTANT: suffix we used puts it on the space-prefixed Yes/ No pair. 3. Prefer the tokenizer-derived single-token logit readout. It depends only on the logit vector, never on what text generation loop returns. String parsing is equivalent to it (Theorem 1, Appendix D) only when it reads exactly the first generated token, which is where InstructBLIP broke. 4. Release prediction-level records so reviewers can recompute any aggregate and check the readout convention independently. Listing 1 is the readout we recommend. It derives the yes/no IDs from the models own tokenizer, generates one token, and compares the max-logits, so the same code runs unchanged across all five models here. It adds no generation cost beyond encoding four short strings once at setup. Listing 1: Drop-in POPE answer readout. Derive the yes/no token IDs from the models own tokenizer, then compare first-token max-logits. sections.title: 7 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.content: The mismatch we report has narrow technical surface: one logit comparison between two IDs that LLaVA-1.5-7B does not produce after ASSISTANT: under greedy decoding. The reach of that mistake depends on which methods adopt the two-token readout. On POPE adversarial F1 the shift to the eight-token readout is 6.13 points, larger than the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of those papers states its readout, so we cannot say which of their baselines the artifact touches, and we estimate no corrected gains. Our 82.21 reference also ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so setting it beside baselines measured at higher precision would mix readout and precision effects. No method is shown to be broken here. Numbers from different studies cannot be 7 compared at face value until the readout and the precision are matched and reported. The correction is one-line change in the evaluation code. few caveats bound the result. The main 9,000-question audit uses one checkpoint at one quantization level (4-bit NF4), so we cannot say whether the 6.13-point shift is the same at higher precision. The nine corrections (Appendix F) were run only on the adversarial split. The whitespace-prefix behaviour is shared across LLaMA-family tokenizers, but the specific IDs differ by vocabulary, so it is the diagnostic in Algorithm 1, not the fixed eight-token set, that carries the finding to new model. Our nine inference-time corrections did not beat the corrected baseline, and the per-signal analysis suggests the visual-grounding and attention signals those methods rely on do not discriminate the cases the adversarial split is built to query. Beating that baseline may need training-time changes, not decoding-time ones. We encourage future POPE work to verify the first-token behaviour of its specific model-template pairing before fixing readout token set.

The eight-token matrix is close to balanced (TP 1,174, TN 1,318, FP 182, FN 326). Switch to two tokens and the false-positive count jumps from 182 to 842, as 660 true-negative No emissions flip to yes; the other 264 of the 924 flipped emissions land on borderline true-yes questions and become true positives, which is why precision drops while recall climbs. Figure 3 tracks the running yes-rate of each protocol over the 3,000-question adversarial stream. Formal Equivalence of String-Parse and Single-Token Readouts The observation that dynamic_single and string_parse agree to four decimals on every run is not coincidence. Under greedy decoding the two protocols are identical whenever the argmax token belongs to the single-token surface-form set, outside the tie case of Theorem 1. Writing the proof down turns an empirical regularity into claim the rest of the paper can lean on. Theorem 1 (Single-token readout equivalence). Let be models vocabulary and let V, be disjoint single-token surface-form sets for the yes and no answers. Let ℓ RV be the first-position logit vector on fixed input, and = arg maxv ℓv the greedy argmax token. Define (cid:20) ˆylogit = 1 max iY ℓi > max jN ℓj (cid:21) , ˆystr = 1[ decode(t) yes-strings ]. If then ˆylogit = ˆystr, unless the maximum is tied between and with its lowest tied ID in . Proof. Greedy decoding emits as the first token, and decode returns the surface form whose vocabulary id is t. By construction holds exactly the single-token yes forms and the singletoken no forms. Suppose . Then ℓt ℓv for every V, so ℓt maxjN ℓj, and ℓt = maxiY ℓi since . The strict inequality maxY ℓ > maxN ℓ holds unless the maximum is tied between and , in which case greedy decoding returns the lowest tied ID, here , while the strict rule returns no; this is the exception in the statement. For the two IDs LLaVA-1.5 emits, 1939 precedes 3869, so tie between them gives = 1939 , the case below. Exact ties do occur, because the logits are fp16 values: in the instrumented adversarial pass (Appendix F.3) the yes-set and no-set maxima are equal on 8 of the 3,000 questions, while the main sweeps records hold no logits, so ties there cannot be counted. Outside tie between and , therefore, ˆylogit = 1 and ˆystr = 1. The case needs no exception: then maxN ℓ = ℓt maxY ℓ, so the strict rule returns no even on tie, and both readouts give 0. On question whose greedy argmax satisfies (Y ) (Y2 N2), the readout ˆylogit(Y2, N2) compares two candidates the decoder did not select. Greedy decoding does not fix which of the two is larger, so the readouts decision is not tied to the emitted answer: for every such there are logit vectors with argmax on which ˆylogit(Y2, N2) = ˆystr, and others on which the two differ. Proof. If Y2 N2, both readouts agree by Theorem 1 applied to (Y2, N2), outside the tie case it excludes. Now let (Y ) (Y2 N2). The argmax condition requires only ℓt ℓv for every V; it places no constraint on the order of the logits inside Y2 N2. Pick Y2 and N2 (disjoint, because and are) and set ℓt = 0, ℓa = 1, ℓb = 2 and ℓv = 3 for every other v. Then is the argmax and ˆylogit(Y2, N2) = 1. Swapping the values at and leaves the argmax and gives ˆylogit(Y2, N2) = 0. Since ˆystr depends on alone, it equals the readout in exactly one of the two cases. The corollary says nothing about how large the excluded logits are or how often the readout agrees in practice; agreement is an empirical property of the model and template. The LLaVA-1.5 audit sits 14 entirely in the second case. The generated token is always 3869 or 1939, and the two-token readout uses Y2 = {3582}, N2 = {1217}, so (Y ) (Y2 N2) covers all 9,000 questions and Theorem 1 guarantees nothing about the two-token decision on any of them. On the records the readout agrees with the emitted answer on 2,076, 2,183 and 2,302 of the 3,000 questions in the adversarial, popular and random splits (0.692, 0.728, 0.767). The agreement is lopsided. It is complete on the 3,893 Yes emissions and partial on No emissions, where ℓ3582 > ℓ1217 on 0.81 of the label-yes questions and on 0.307 to 0.501 of the label-no ones  (Table 7)  . That asymmetry is what inflates the two-token yes-rate to 0.760 on adversarial, and it indicates that the excluded logits may track the models lean. Across the multi-model runs the dynamic_single and string_parse readouts report identical F1, precision, recall, and yes-rate to four decimals on LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B, mPLUG-Owl2, and Qwen2-VL. On InstructBLIP they disagree, and the disagreement does not contradict Theorem 1: the theorem equates the logit readout with parsing decode(t), single token, whereas string parsing here scanned up to six generated tokens of free text whose leading span did not begin with the answer token. Inference-Time Correction Experiments With the baseline pinned at 0.8221, we asked simple question: can any inference-time signal push past it on the adversarial split? Over roughly 90 GPU-hours we ran nine variants, six grounding-based and three contrastive. None improved adversarial F1. Section F.3 below reports the per-question diagnostics that explain why. F.1 Methods tested All nine variants act on the answer-position logits, before the eight-token decision rule. Six suppress yes-logits when an external visual-uncertainty signal is low; one applies uniform suppression as control; two use contrastive image variants. Where relevant we sweep the suppression strength β. CLIP-B/32 certainty gating. Cosine similarity between CLIP-ViT-B/32 [Radford et al., 2021] patch features and the question-noun embedding gives certainty in [0, 1], used to scale yessuppression as ℓmod yes = ℓyes β(1 c), with β {1.0, 1.5}. CLIP-L/14-336 certainty gating. Same procedure with the larger CLIP-L, using patch features through its visual projection head, so the embedding space matches LLaVA-1.5s own vision tower. Entropy gating. Answer-position token-distribution entropy, normalised to [0, 1]; higher entropy means lower certainty and stronger suppression. Magnitude gating. The relative magnitude of the yes-token logit in the full vocabulary distribution, used as soft suppression threshold. CLS feature similarity. Cosine similarity between the CLIP-ViT-L/14-336 CLS embedding and the question-noun text embedding. Object-noun CLIP similarity. Full-image CLIP-B/32 embedding against the question-noun embedding, with rule-based noun extraction from the question template. Uniform yes-suppression. control that applies fixed suppression to every question, to quantify how much movement is signal-driven versus static yes-bias correction. Generation midpoint gating. The yes/no logit gap read at an intermediate generation step rather than the final position. VCD-noise perturbation. Following Leng et al. [2024], second forward pass with Gaussian noise on the image embedding gives contrastive logit set; the decision is taken on the difference. F.2 Results Table 8 reports F1, precision, and recall for all nine. Figure 7 sorts them by F1 and places them on the precision-recall plane. Every yes-suppression variant buys 1.5 to 6.0 precision points at cost of 3.0 to 5.8 recall points, and in no case is the precision gain enough to cover the recall loss. The baseline splits into 1,173 TPs, 1,317 TNs, 183 FPs, and 327 FNs (2,490 correct, 510 wrong). This diagnostic was separate instrumented run, and it differs from the main sweep (1,174 / 1,318 / 182 / 326) on 2 of the 3,000 questions, both fp16 ties or near-ties: on ID 77 (label yes) the yes-set and no-set maxima are both 24.6875 and the diagnostics strict-inequality rule answers no, and on ID 2938 (label no) the yes-set maximum leads by 0.0156, one fp16 step at this magnitude. Three signals carry most of the weight. 16 (a) F1 ordered against baseline. (b) Precisionrecall plane. Figure 7: Nine inference-time corrections on POPE adversarial, two views. (a) F1 against the corrected baseline at 0.8221. (b) The same methods on the precision-recall plane with F1 iso-curves. Every yes-suppression variant moves north and west of the baseline; no path crosses the F1=0.8221 iso-curve. CLIP-L similarity separates TPs from FPs by small but reliable margin. We took the maximum cosine similarity between the question-noun text embedding and CLIP-Ls 576 patch features for every question. The TP group (n=1,173) has mean 0.1507 and the FP group (n=183) has mean 0.1375, gap of 0.0132 (95% bootstrap CI [0.0084, 0.0180], 10,000 resamples, percentile method, NumPy default_rng seed 42; MannWhitney = 132923, = 2.05 107; Cohens = 0.40). Reliable but small. gate keyed on this signal would have to separate TPs from FPs at = 0.40 while the precision-recall tradeoff punishes any threshold that suppresses FPs at the expense of TPs. The pattern fits structural property of the split: adversarial negatives co-occur in the same image as the queried object, CLIP was trained on the same co-occurrence statistics, and its embedding space encodes them. Decoder attention points the wrong way. Mean attention from the final text token to the 576 image positions, averaged across layers 1420, is 0.0738 for correct predictions (n=2,490) and 0.0801 for wrong ones (n=510); MannWhitney = 452635, two-sided = 1.45 1024, Cohens = 0.46. The layers-1420 window was fixed before analysis as the mid-to-late band of the 32-layer LLaMA-2 decoder, not tuned to maximise the effect. The direction holds per category: FPs show higher mean attention (0.0833) than TPs (0.0780; = 4.13 109), and FNs higher (0.0783) than TNs (0.0700; = 1.50 1023). Wrong predictions consistently draw more image attention than correct ones (Figure 8). plausible reading is that uncertain predictions trigger more looking as the model hunts for evidence, which runs against the more grounding means more correct assumption the six grounding gates rely on. The logit gap separates by confidence, not correctness. Figure 9 gives the mean absolute logit gap ℓyes ℓno per category: 2.066 for TPs, 1.482 for TNs, 0.700 for FPs, and 0.962 for FNs. It separates correct from wrong with Cohens = 1.06 across all 3,000 questions (p = 1.22 1093). Within the positive class TPs beat FNs (d = 1.22, = 4.83 1068); within the negative class TNs beat FPs (d = 1.18, = 1.19 1041). The model is most confident when right and least confident when wrong. Suppression acts on small-gap questions in both directions at once: small-gap TP gets pushed to FN at roughly the rate small-gap FP gets pushed to TN, so the net F1 contribution is near zero, and in our runs the sign came out negative every time. The p-values here are uncorrected for multiple comparisons; given the effect magnitudes, Bonferroni correction over the six tests changes no qualitative conclusion. The adversarial split is behaving as designed. Co-occurring negatives are hard to refute with image evidence, because the evidence ambiguously supports both the queried object and the one actually present. The methods we tested assume separable correctness signal the split is built to deny. On the easier splits we would expect the same suppression to look better, since those negatives are easier Figure 8: Distribution of mean attention from the final text token to image positions, layers 1420, on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Blue bars are correct (n=2490); red bars are wrong (n=510). Higher image attention associates with wrong predictions, so suppressing yes-logits when attention is low removes signal from the wrong side of the distribution. Figure 9: Absolute logit gap ℓyes ℓno at the answer position on the 3,000-question adversarial run. Left: per-category mean with one-standard-deviation error bars (TP n=1173, TN n=1317, FP n=183, FN n=327; means 2.07, 1.48, 0.70, 0.96). Right: kernel-density estimates. The order TP > TN > FN > FP at the mean separates confidence from correctness, which is why uncertainty-keyed corrections trade TPs for FNs at about the same rate as FPs for TNs. to rule out visually. G.2 Prompt-template robustness The master table fixes one template per model. To check the dynamic readout is stable under template change, rather than an artifact of the LLaVA-1.5 string, we compared the first 500 POPE adversarial questions of LLaVA-1.6-Mistral under two templates: the LLaVA-1.5 paper template and the models native chat template via processor.apply_chat_template. In both runs the only first tokens generated were id 5592 (Yes) and id 1770 (No); the LLaMA-2 IDs never appeared. Table 11 reports the four readouts. The dynamic single-token and string-parse readouts agree to four decimals under either template, the empirical face of Theorem 1. The legacy eight-token readout is 0 under both, because none of the LLaMA-2 IDs is ever the argmax on Mistral vocabulary, and the comparison between two zero-mass logits resolves the same way on every question. Absolute F1 is not comparable to LLaVA-1.5: on the full 3,000-question split the dynamic readout gives 0.8521, and the 0.8719 here is the 500-question slice. The point of the cross-model run is narrow, that the framework ports cleanly when token sets are re-derived from each models tokenizer, and that transferring the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim is unsafe. and verification. sections.content: This section scopes the finding honestly: the published numbers below cannot be placed on our scale, because no surveyed paper states its readout and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization. Table 12 lists the papers we have inspected that report LLaVA-1.5-7B POPE adversarial baseline. Every surveyed paper leaves its readout not stated, so none can be confirmed from released code or explicit statement, and the number of papers whose readout we can verify is zero. We therefore report no ratio over 20 verified readouts. Inferring readout from baseline value would break our own rule, and substituting our 82.21 for papers baseline would not estimate corrected gain: our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, and published baseline may differ from it in readout, precision, prompt format, or decoding. The adversarial baselines in Table 12 run from 73.54 to 82.07, spread of 8.53 points that these papers do not let us decompose. Settling the comparison takes matched reruns of each method with the readout logged and the precision fixed, or at least the readout stated in the paper or its code. Expanding the survey means reading each papers evaluation code rather than inferring the readout.
